problem: Open-vocabulary embedding maps (OpenScene, OpenMask3D, CLIP viewpoint stores) are implicit: they cannot report which entities they contain, need queries to be guessed, and are memory heavy. Explicit maps with fixed classes are too limited to ground LLMs on open-ended tasks.
motivation: LLMs need scene context to produce actionable plans, especially for tasks that do not name a goal object. A text-based, explicit map can be inserted directly into the LLM prompt, so the LLM can pick relevant entities itself. Image tagging models already recognize thousands of classes, which suggests a very compact text map is possible.
key_idea: Store per-viewpoint text tags from a multi-label image tagging model (RAM) with camera poses and depth statistics, localize tags in 3D by voting over viewpoint frusta, and expose the tag list and a localization API to an LLM.
insight: Tags plus multi-view frustum voting give coarse localizations comparable to embedding maps (object precision at 1.0 m 0.46 vs 0.41, recall 0.65 vs 0.61/0.41) with orders of magnitude less memory. Tag-based viewpoint retrieval beats CLIP retrieval in precision (and in object recall), suggesting specialized recognition models beat generic embeddings for this purpose. The crop-ensemble filter is the module that matters: removing it drops object precision (e.g. 0.45→0.39 at 1.0 m) for a small recall gain, while the depth filter has negligible effect.
method: Tag map: hash table from unique tags to viewpoints; each viewpoint stores ID, camera pose and a depth statistic (80th percentile far-plane distance); no images stored.
Construction filters: discard close-up frames via mean/median depth threshold (0.6 m); crop-augmented ensemble of RAM (5% and 10% border crops) keeps only tags agreed upon by all members.

Coarse localization: for a tag, build the frustum of every viewpoint that has it, voxelize (0.2 m), count votes per voxel, threshold at several normalized levels (0, .25, .5, .75), cluster with DBSCAN, then apply NMS to remove proposals containing higher-confidence ones.

LLM grounding: append the list of unique tags to the GPT-4 prompt and provide function-calling API (localize_tag, region_region_dist, point_region_dist) so the LLM builds spatial relations on demand; the prompt tells it tags are noisy and to cite confidence.

Evaluation metrics: P2E (proposal-to-entity) and E2P (entity-to-proposal) expected shortest path lengths, approximated on a 0.5 m grid graph, giving Precision/Recall at threshold (equivalent to a directed average Hausdorff distance).
Real-robot pipeline: ANYmal with a COLMAP-built map, a pose graph for global paths, and a local planner; chat interface supports clarification and follow-up tasks.

setting.backbone: RAM (ram_swin_large, pretrained tagging model, frozen) + GPT-4 (frozen, function calling)
setting.training_data: none (training-free; uses pretrained RAM and GPT-4)
setting.observation: posed RGB-D viewpoints (Matterport3D views for evaluation; COLMAP-posed RGB-D for the real scene)
setting.action_space: LLM selects coarse 3D goal regions; a pose graph and local planner execute paths on the ANYmal legged robot
setting.simulator: Matterport3D dataset (offline localization evaluation, no simulator); real world
setting.privileged: Offline pre-collected viewpoints with known poses (dataset poses / COLMAP) for map construction; GT meshes and labels only for the evaluation metric; static scene assumed.

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark (SR/SPL) is reported; the metrics are localization precision/recall. Memory comparison and CLIP comparison are given only in figures.
results: Tag map localizations match or beat OpenScene and OpenMask3D for objects at most thresholds (precision@1.0m 0.46 vs 0.41/0.41, recall@1.0m 0.65 vs 0.61/0.41) while using two to four orders of magnitude less memory. For regions, OpenMask3D has the best precision and OpenScene the best recall, with the tag map in between on precision and lowest recall at small thresholds. With GPT-4, the map grounded navigation succeeded on 21/25 lab queries, with failures mostly from tagging false positives.
limitations: Tagging false positives pollute the LLM context and cause infeasible plans (e.g., fire alarm tagged as mailbox); localizations are coarse, with worse precision at small thresholds.
Static scenes only; viewpoint collection strategy is not studied; evaluated with dataset-provided viewpoints.
Real-robot evaluation is small (25 queries, one lab scene) and there is no standard ObjectNav benchmark evaluation.
